title: Hanuman's counsel
hook: to comfort Sita, the monkey who just crossed an ocean tells her he's the weakest of Sugriva's army
carry: none in the army weaker than me

segments.voice: Yesterday: her doubt. Even when Hanuman grew like a mountain, Sita said no, for safety, choice and Rama's honor. Your line: a decision, not a doubt.

Hanuman has to leave Sita in the grove. She's chosen to wait for Rama. Goodbyes like this are the hardest part: you're leaving, they're staying, and you want to say something that lasts after you've gone. Before he goes, she gives him tokens to take back, and he gives her something too: his counsel. A few sentences meant to hold her up until help arrives.
screen: `THE HARDEST PART IS THE GOODBYE.` → `TOKENS FOR RAMA.` → `COUNSEL FOR SITA.`

segments.voice: First, Sita's tokens. She tells Hanuman a private memory only Rama would know. One day at Chitrakuta a crow kept attacking her, and Rama, angry, sent a single blade of grass after it, charged with divine power; the crow found no shelter anywhere until it came back and fell at Rama's feet. Tell him that, she says, and he'll know you met me. Then she unties a jewel from her hair, the chudamani, and gives it to him. And she says plainly that she can hold on only for a month. Then Hanuman counsels her. Don't grieve. Rama and Lakshmana will come soon with Sugriva's army; they will burn Lanka and take you home. And because Sita has asked how monkeys could ever cross this ocean, he adds something surprising. There are many in Sugriva's army stronger than me, and none weaker. If I could cross, how much more easily can they? The monkey who leapt a hundred yojanas, fought Simhika and talked his way past Surasa calls himself the least of the army. Is it true? The story has shown his strength; it's hard to believe. But that's not the point. If Hanuman is the strongest, the rescue depends on one monkey. If he's the weakest, help is enormous, and coming. He makes himself small, so her hope can be large: words shaped to what she most fears.
screen: `THE CROW AND THE BLADE OF GRASS.` · `THE JEWEL FROM HER HAIR.` · `DON'T GRIEVE; RAMA WILL COME.` · then, large: `NONE IN THE ARMY IS WEAKER THAN ME.`

segments.voice: Hold in mind someone who's waiting for something hard, a diagnosis, a verdict, a return, and gently notice what they most fear. Let a few simple, true words of comfort form, shaped not to what you want to say but to that fear, and breathe them in and out slowly until they feel right.
Hanuman's counsel. His words to Sita before leaving: don't grieve, Rama will come, and there are many in the army stronger than me, and none weaker.
Your line: none in the army weaker than me. Tomorrow, Hanuman counsels himself. Day six hundred twenty-four, done.

howItsDone: The chudamani, Sita's hair jewel, is a familiar element in Ramayana art and storytelling, and Hanuman's words of reassurance to Sita are often recited by devotees as words of comfort in hard times.

fork.setup: you're Hanuman. Sita fears no army could cross this sea. you just did it alone. what do you tell her?
options: only I could do it, so it's hopeless.
many in the army are stronger than me, and none weaker.
fork.reveal: Hanuman calls himself the least of Sugriva's army, so that Sita sees the rescue as certain, not a one-monkey miracle.

original.note: Sanskrit cūḍāmaṇi, crest jewel: cūḍā, the crown of the head, and maṇi, jewel.

trapdoor: what you thought: Hanuman's counsel is just 'don't worry'.
what it means: he shapes his words to Sita's fear, even making himself the least of the army.
what a scholar hears: Sita's crow story (the kākāsura episode) is a private memory that works as a recognition token, a device the epic uses alongside the physical tokens of ring and jewel.

chat.says: Hanuman was super strong. Why did he tell Sita he was the weakest in the army?
options: So her hope could be large: if the weakest crossed, the rest easily could.
Because he was too tired from the leap to feel strong anymore.
Because Sita had asked him not to boast in Ravana's garden.
chat.meaning: Hanuman shaped his words to Sita's fear. If he's the weakest, help is enormous and coming, not hanging on one monkey.

Chitrakuta.meaning: the forest mountain where Rama and Sita once lived

chudamani.meaning: a crest jewel worn in the hair

Simhika.meaning: a sea demon who seized creatures by their shadows

yojanas.meaning: an old Indian measure of distance, many miles each

sources.ref: Valmiki Ramayana, Sundara Kanda 38 (the crow at Chitrakuta; the chudamani; one month)
Valmiki Ramayana, Sundara Kanda 39 (Hanuman reassures Sita; none weaker than me)

notes: Crow story details: the crow is identified in some tellings as Indra's son (Jayanta / Kakasura); the script avoids naming him and omits the loss of the crow's eye. Confirm.
Sita's 'one month' (that she will live only a month more): confirm Sundara 38.
Hanuman's statement that there are many stronger and none weaker than him in Sugriva's army: confirm (Sundara 39).

Title note: 'Hanuman's counsel' is read here as his counsel to Sita (day 624) and his own counsel with himself (day 625); his counsel to Ravana (Sundara 51) falls in 'the fight' (day 627). A Keeper may prefer a different split.
